Base directory for this skill: /Users/evisdrenova/.claude/plugins/cache/claude-plugins-official/superpowers/6.4.1/skills/brainstorming

# Brainstorming Ideas Into Designs

Help turn ideas into fully formed designs and specs through natural collaborative dialogue.

Start by classifying how much process the request needs, then work
through your path: understand the context, refine the idea, present a
design, and get your human partner's approval.

## Establish Shared Understanding

The outcome of brainstorming is an understanding your human partner can
recognize and correct, grounded in what they want to accomplish.

1. **Discover intent.** Use the request and available context to identify
   the intended outcome, who it is for, and what success looks like. When
   that information is missing, ask one focused question about purpose or
   intended use before proposing features or an approach. Knowing the app
   genre does not tell you why your partner wants it. Gathering missing
   requirements does not ask them to authorize the task again.
2. **Write back your understanding.** Summarize the intended outcome,
   relevant constraints, and success criteria in a short note your partner
   can assess. Separate what they said from assumptions. Invite correction
   and incorporate their answer before treating this as the design brief.
3. **Carry intent into the design.** Preserve the agreed understanding in
   the selected path's design artifact: the written spec for architectural
   work, or the in-chat design/probe for bounded work and spikes. Check
   proposed features and technical choices against that understanding.

When the request already supplies the purpose and constraints, reflect
that understanding instead of asking the same questions again. Keep the
note concise; its accuracy and the opportunity to correct it matter.

<HARD-GATE>
Before taking any implementation action, including invoking an
implementation skill, writing product code, scaffolding, installing
product dependencies, or creating an external project, complete the
selected path's prerequisites:

- Spike: the human partner approves the question and probe.
- Bounded: the human partner approves the short in-chat design.
- Architectural: the human partner reviews and approves the written spec,
  then reviews the written implementation plan and selects its execution
  method. Conversational design approval only permits writing the spec;
  written-spec approval only permits invoking writing-plans.

A reply approves the stage actually presented. Approval of an idea or
feature scope does not approve artifacts that do not exist yet. Resume
at the earliest incomplete stage; do not turn one approval into permission
to skip the rest of the selected path. Read-only project exploration is
allowed while those prerequisites remain incomplete.
</HARD-GATE>

## Three Paths

Before your first question, classify the request and say the
classification out loud — "this looks bounded, so I'll present a short
design here rather than write a spec" — so your human partner can
override it:

- **Spike** — a feasibility question ("can we...", "is it possible...",
  "quick and dirty is fine") whose output is an answer, not code you
  keep. Present the question and what you'll try in 2-3 sentences, get
  a nod, then find out as cheaply as correctness allows. No design
  doc, no spec file. Report findings as a recommendation; anything you
  built stays labeled throwaway.
- **Bounded** — a well-scoped change to code that already exists in
  this repo: a new flag, a small endpoint, a one-file fix.
  Understanding the kind of app is not enough — bounded means the flow
  you are changing is already here to read. If there is no existing
  flow to change, the task is not bounded. Ask the clarifying
  questions that matter, present a short design IN CHAT (a few
  sentences to a few short paragraphs), and STOP. Implementation
  starts only after your human partner says yes to that design — a
  bounded task's approval is as hard a gate as an architectural
  one. No spec file, no implementation plan document.
- **Architectural** — new projects, new subsystems, changes that
  restructure how components fit together or alter interfaces others
  depend on. Follow the full process: questions, approaches, sectioned
  design, written spec, then the writing-plans skill.

When in doubt between two paths, take the heavier one. The ratchet is
one-way: hidden complexity discovered mid-task upgrades the path —
stop, say so, and step up. Nothing downgrades mid-task.

## Anti-Pattern: "Too Simple To Need Approval"

Every path ends with your human partner approving the required design
before implementation. A bounded change may need only two sentences in
chat. A new todo-list project is architectural and requires the written
spec and planning handoffs. Scale the artifact to the selected path;
complete that path's reviews before implementation.

## Red Flags

| Thought | Reality |
|---------|---------|
| "This is too simple to need a design" | Follow the selected path: a bounded change gets a short chat design; an architectural change gets the written spec and planning handoffs. |
| "I'll call it bounded and skip the spec" | Reaching for a label to skip work IS the doubt — take the heavier path. |
| "It's bounded and the design is obvious — I'll start while they read it" | The gate is the approval, not the design's length. Present, then stop until you hear yes. |
| "I understand this kind of app, so it's bounded" | Bounded measures the repo, not your familiarity. A new project has no existing flow — it is architectural. |
| "The spike works, so I'll keep the code" | A spike's output is an answer. Keeping the code is a new request — classify it. |
| "It grew, but I'm almost done — no need to re-classify" | Hidden complexity upgrades the path mid-task. Stop and say so. |
| "They approved the spike, so the follow-up change is approved too" | Each task gets its own classification and its own approval. |

## Checklist

Classify first, announce the path, then create a task for each item on
your path and complete them in order.

**Spike:**
1. **Explore project context** — enough to frame the probe
2. **Present question + probe plan** — 2-3 sentences
3. **Get approval** — a nod is enough
4. **Investigate** — as cheaply as correctness allows
5. **Report findings** — a recommendation; label anything built as throwaway

**Bounded:**
1. **Explore project context** — check files, docs, recent commits
2. **Ask clarifying questions** — one at a time, the ones that matter
3. **Present short design in chat** — approach, files touched, testing
4. **Get approval** — STOP and wait for an explicit yes; presenting the design and starting in the same breath is skipping the gate
5. **Implement** — proceed with the normal development workflow (TDD applies); no plan document

**Architectural:**
1. **Explore project context** — check files, docs, recent commits
2. **Offer the visual companion just-in-time** — NOT upfront. The first time a question would genuinely be clearer shown than described, offer it then (its own message); on approval its browser tab opens for you. If no visual question ever arises, never offer it. See the Visual Companion section below.
3. **Ask clarifying questions** — one at a time, understand purpose/constraints/success criteria
4. **Propose 2-3 approaches** — with trade-offs and your recommendation
5. **Present design** — in sections scaled to their complexity, get user approval after each section
6. **Write design doc** — save to `docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md` and commit
7. **Spec self-review** — quick inline check for placeholders, contradictions, ambiguity, scope (see below)
8. **User reviews written spec** — ask user to review the spec file before proceeding
9. **Transition to implementation** — invoke writing-plans skill to create implementation plan

## Process Flow

```dot
digraph brainstorming {
    "Classify: spike / bounded / architectural" [shape=diamond];
    "Present question + probe (2-3 sentences)" [shape=box];
    "Ask clarifying questions (bounded)" [shape=box];
    "Present short design in chat" [shape=box];
    "Human approves?" [shape=diamond];
    "Investigate; report recommendation" [shape=doublecircle];
    "Implement via normal workflow (no plan doc)" [shape=doublecircle];
    "Explore project context" [shape=box];
    "Ask clarifying questions" [shape=box];
    "Propose 2-3 approaches" [shape=box];
    "Present design sections" [shape=box];
    "User approves design?" [shape=diamond];
    "Write design doc" [shape=box];
    "Spec self-review\n(fix inline)" [shape=box];
    "User reviews spec?" [shape=diamond];
    "Invoke writing-plans skill" [shape=doublecircle];
    "Hidden complexity? Upgrade path" [shape=box];

    "Classify: spike / bounded / architectural" -> "Present question + probe (2-3 sentences)" [label="spike"];
    "Classify: spike / bounded / architectural" -> "Ask clarifying questions (bounded)" [label="bounded"];
    "Classify: spike / bounded / architectural" -> "Explore project context" [label="architectural"];
    "Present question + probe (2-3 sentences)" -> "Human approves?";
    "Ask clarifying questions (bounded)" -> "Present short design in chat";
    "Present short design in chat" -> "Human approves?";
    "Human approves?" -> "Investigate; report recommendation" [label="spike: yes"];
    "Human approves?" -> "Implement via normal workflow (no plan doc)" [label="bounded: yes"];
    "Hidden complexity? Upgrade path" -> "Classify: spike / bounded / architectural";
    "Explore project context" -> "Ask clarifying questions";
    "Ask clarifying questions" -> "Propose 2-3 approaches";
    "Propose 2-3 approaches" -> "Present design sections";
    "Present design sections" -> "User approves design?";
    "User approves design?" -> "Present design sections" [label="no, revise"];
    "User approves design?" -> "Write design doc" [label="yes"];
    "Write design doc" -> "Spec self-review\n(fix inline)";
    "Spec self-review\n(fix inline)" -> "User reviews spec?";
    "User reviews spec?" -> "Write design doc" [label="changes requested"];
    "User reviews spec?" -> "Invoke writing-plans skill" [label="approved"];
}
```

**Terminal states are path-bound.** Architectural: the ONLY skill you
invoke after brainstorming is writing-plans — never frontend-design,
mcp-builder, or any other implementation skill. Bounded: after
approval, implementation proceeds directly through the normal
development workflow; no plan document. Spike: the terminal state is a
reported recommendation.

## The Process

The subsections below serve the bounded and architectural paths (a
spike stops at "present the probe, get a nod"). Sections from
**Exploring approaches** onward are architectural-path depth — for
bounded work, context plus a few questions plus a short in-chat design
is the whole process.

**Understanding the idea:**

- Check out the current project state first (files, docs, recent commits)
- Before asking detailed questions, assess scope: if the request describes multiple independent subsystems (e.g., "build a platform with chat, file storage, billing, and analytics"), flag this immediately. Don't spend questions refining details of a project that needs to be decomposed first.
- If the project is too large for a single spec, help the user decompose into sub-projects: what are the independent pieces, how do they relate, what order should they be built? Then brainstorm the first sub-project through the normal design flow. Each sub-project gets its own spec → plan → implementation cycle.
- For appropriately-scoped projects, ask questions one at a time to refine the idea
- Prefer multiple choice questions when possible, but open-ended is fine too
- Only one question per message - if a topic needs more exploration, break it into multiple questions
- Focus on understanding: purpose, constraints, success criteria

**Exploring approaches:**

- Propose 2-3 different approaches with trade-offs
- Present options conversationally with your recommendation and reasoning
- Lead with your recommended option and explain why
- YAGNI ruthlessly - remove unnecessary features from every approach and design

**Presenting the design:**

- Once you believe you understand what you're building, present the design
- Scale each section to its complexity: a few sentences if straightforward, up to 200-300 words if nuanced
- Ask after each section whether it looks right so far
- Cover: architecture, components, data flow, error handling, testing
- Be ready to go back and clarify if something doesn't make sense

**Design for isolation and clarity:**

- Break the system into smaller units that each have one clear purpose, communicate through well-defined interfaces, and can be understood and tested independently
- For each unit, you should be able to answer: what does it do, how do you use it, and what does it depend on?
- Can someone understand what a unit does without reading its internals? Can you change the internals without breaking consumers? If not, the boundaries need work.
- Smaller, well-bounded units are also easier for you to work with - you reason better about code you can hold in context at once, and your edits are more reliable when files are focused. When a file grows large, that's often a signal that it's doing too much.

**Working in existing codebases:**

- Explore the current structure before proposing changes. Follow existing patterns.
- Where existing code has problems that affect the work (e.g., a file that's grown too large, unclear boundaries, tangled responsibilities), include targeted improvements as part of the design - the way a good developer improves code they're working in.
- Don't propose unrelated refactoring. Stay focused on what serves the current goal.

## After the Design (architectural path)

**Documentation:**

- Write the validated design (spec) to `docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md`
  - (User preferences for spec location override this default)
- Use elements-of-style:writing-clearly-and-concisely skill if available
- Commit the design document to git

**Spec Self-Review:**
After writing the spec document, look at it with fresh eyes:

1. **Placeholder scan:** Any "TBD", "TODO", incomplete sections, or vague requirements? Fix them.
2. **Internal consistency:** Do any sections contradict each other? Does the architecture match the feature descriptions?
3. **Scope check:** Is this focused enough for a single implementation plan, or does it need decomposition?
4. **Ambiguity check:** Could any requirement be interpreted two different ways? If so, pick one and make it explicit.

Fix any issues inline. No need to re-review — just fix and move on.

**User Review Gate:**
After the spec review loop passes, ask the user to review the written spec before proceeding:

> "Spec written and committed to `<path>`. Please review it and let me know if you want to make any changes before we start writing out the implementation plan."

Wait for the user's response. If they request changes, make them and re-run the spec review loop. Only proceed once the user approves.

**Implementation:**

- Invoke the writing-plans skill to create a detailed implementation plan
- Do NOT invoke any other skill. writing-plans is the next step.

## Visual Companion

A browser-based companion for showing mockups, diagrams, and visual options during brainstorming. Available as a tool — not a mode. Accepting the companion means it's available for questions that benefit from visual treatment; it does NOT mean every question goes through the browser.

**Offering the companion (just-in-time):** Do NOT offer it upfront. Wait until a question would genuinely be clearer shown than told — a real mockup / layout / diagram question, not merely a UI *topic*. The first time that happens, offer it then, as its own message:
> "This next part might be easier if I show you — I can put together mockups, diagrams, and comparisons in a browser tab as we go. It's still new and can be token-intensive. Want me to? I'll open it for you."

**This offer MUST be its own message.** Only the offer — no clarifying question, summary, or other content. Wait for the user's response. If they accept, start the server with `--open` so their browser opens to the first screen automatically. If they decline, continue text-only and don't offer again unless they raise it.

**Per-question decision:** Even after the user accepts, decide FOR EACH QUESTION whether to use the browser or the terminal. The test: **would the user understand this better by seeing it than reading it?**

- **Use the browser** for content that IS visual — mockups, wireframes, layout comparisons, architecture diagrams, side-by-side visual designs
- **Use the terminal** for content that is text — requirements questions, conceptual choices, tradeoff lists, A/B/C/D text options, scope decisions

A question about a UI topic is not automatically a visual question. "What does personality mean in this context?" is a conceptual question — use the terminal. "Which wizard layout works better?" is a visual question — use the browser.

If they agree to the companion, read the detailed guide before proceeding:
`skills/brainstorming/visual-companion.md`

# Benchmarks

Selected measurements of Brain, their limits, and commands for evaluating your
own repository. Historical results include both gains and closed negatives.

**What this page is not:** a head-to-head against another memory product. We
have not run one under conditions we would defend, and [saying so](#head-to-head-against-other-products)
is more useful than a number nobody can reproduce.

## Run it yourself

You should not have to take our numbers on trust. These two need no
configuration, no API key and no network, and run against whatever repository
you point them at:

```sh
entire brain bench scale        # index size and query latency vs codebase size
entire brain bench semantic     # indexing throughput and memory
```

Both require a clean worktree — the indexer refuses uncommitted content — and
`--json` emits the full record.

Retrieval quality needs a task set, because a quality number without one is a
number about nothing:

```sh
entire brain facts eval-gen --out tasks.json     # build a task set from this brain
entire brain facts eval --tasks tasks.json       # deterministic when tasks carry labels
entire brain facts eval-compare --a <a.json> --b <b.json>
```

`facts eval` is deterministic and model-free when the task set carries relevance
labels. It calls an agent only if you pass `--judge`, which asks a model to
label relevance instead — that costs tokens, and it is opt-in for exactly that
reason.

## Scale: historical measurements

These September 2026 summaries cover five repositories from 174k to 4.8M lines
on one Apple M-series laptop, using the `syntax-only` profile. They describe the
original benchmark, not the current build. Raw per-query samples and exact
corpus revisions were not retained; these rows cannot be independently
reproduced byte-for-byte.

| Repository | kLOC | Index | KB/kLOC | code search p50 |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| entire-api | 174 | 40 MB | 237 | 299 ms |
| entire.io | 485 | 103 MB | 218 | 1,329 ms |
| entiredb | 628 | 112 MB | 183 | 1,407 ms |

# Memory ladder

A small, reproducible comparison of what a coding agent can answer about a
repository's past as you add memory surfaces one step at a time:

| Cond | Agent has | Guide the agent receives |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | source tree and git history | plain note; no Entire tooling |
| 2 | + hosted session history (`entire search`, `entire checkpoint explain --full`) | plain note + session section |
| 3 | + Graph (`entire graph query`, `neighbors`, `impact`) | `entire graph agent-guide` rendered outside a repository (standalone Graph) + session section |
| 4 | + Brain, normal guidance | Brain's `agent-guide --normal` rendered inside this repository (combined Graph and Brain) + session section |
| 5 | + Brain, strict guidance | this repository's committed `.entire/agent-guide.md` + session section |

Every condition runs the same prompt against a fresh clone with the same
read-only tool allowlist. The harness directory itself (prompt, rubric, this
README) is removed from the clone's worktree and HEAD tree before the agent
starts, so it cannot read its own answer key. Once the harness has merged it still
exists in history, so the agent's `git` is also a shim (`bin/git`): read
subcommands only, any argument naming the directory refused, and a pathspec
exclusion appended to history and content readers so `git show <sha>` and
`git log -p` cannot print its diff even for the commits that added it. Mixed
commits can still expose harness details in their messages. `parse.py` records
any probe for the directory and marks a run contaminated if a tool result
carries harness identifiers (including commit metadata), rubric or README
content; `grade.py` excludes those. The clone's
HEAD is one commit past the indexed commit, and Brain's freshness label moves from
"degraded" to "unsafe"; its facts and history sections are unchanged by that
(checked: 3 facts and 3 history matches before and after). A shim first on `PATH` decides which `entire`
subcommands exist, so an agent cannot reach a surface its condition excludes,
and lifecycle hooks are swallowed so nested runs never capture checkpoints. The
guides are generated from the product at run time, not checked in.

The question is the kind a product manager asks, not an engineer: "should we
auto-activate Brain on global install, and was this decided before?" Its
recorded answer exists only in agent session history and as a Brain
closed-negative fact, not in code, docs or commit messages.

## Run it

Requirements: `claude` (Claude Code CLI), `entire` logged in (hosted search needs
it), `entire graph` and `entire brain` plugins installed, a clean checkout.

```sh
benchmarks/memory-ladder/run-all.sh            # 3 reps x 5 conditions, sequential, then grade
benchmarks/memory-ladder/run.sh 2 1            # one condition, one rep
python3 benchmarks/memory-ladder/grade.py      # table of runs and per-condition means
```

The clone is single-branch and non-local: the source repository carries Entire's
checkpoint refs, whose commits are session transcripts (including those of the
sessions that built this harness and quote its answer key), and a default clone
would expose them to every condition through `git log --all`. Only the branch
under test and tags are fetched, and the checkpoint objects are not transferred.

The agent is confined to its clone. Measured against this Claude Code build:
Bash file commands (`cat`, `find`, `ls`, `grep`) on a path outside the working
directory are blocked by the runtime; the Read tool is not, so it is granted only
as `Read(./**)`; the Grep and Glob tools are not path-scoped by permission rules,
so they are not granted and the agent uses `grep`, `rg`, `find` and `ls` through
the sandboxed shell; the Agent tool launches regardless of the allowlist and
cannot be scoped to one subagent type, so it is denied (subagents inherited the
parent's rules when measured, and no run so far launched one). Runs land in `$TMPDIR/memory-ladder-runs` by default and
`run.sh` refuses an output directory inside this repository, so the clone never
sits a relative path away from the un-stripped harness. `parse.py` records every
tool input that names a path outside the clone and marks a run contaminated if
one reaches the source repository.

Knobs: `LADDER_BRAIN_BIN` (an `entire-brain` binary to run instead of the
installed plugin for conditions 4 and 5, for example a build from `main`; it
reads the installed store and also renders condition 4's guide), `LADDER_MODEL`
(default `sonnet`), `LADDER_MAX_TURNS` (80), `LADDER_OUT`
(default `$TMPDIR/memory-ladder-runs`, must be outside this repository), `LADDER_ORIGIN` (clone origin URL; Brain and
Graph derive the repository key from it, so keep the GitHub URL), `LADDER_BRANCH`
(default `main`; Brain scopes facts to the checked-out branch, so a clone of a
feature branch sees no facts at all). Graph prewarm
for conditions 3 and above is excluded from timing and recorded in `prewarm.txt`.

Each run leaves `stream.jsonl` (the full agent transcript), `summary.json`
(metrics, completion state, every shell command, the final answer, the clone's
HEAD) and the clone it ran in. `grade.py` averages completed runs only and lists

**100M lines has not been measured.** No competitor implementation was run
under this workload. Full method, variance and caveats are in [scale](scale.md).

## Retrieval quality: what moved the numbers

These are Brain measured against Brain — one retrieval arm against another on
the same corpus and task set. They are not comparisons with other products.

| Finding | Evidence | Outcome |
| --- | --- | --- |
| BM25 over substring matching on history | 2.7x–5.1x useful/1k across strata on entire-cli; BM25 gains also observed on two other repositories | BM25 is the no-embedder default |
| EmbeddingGemma fusion over BM25 | +13% useful/1k (t=7.08) and precision +0.016 (t=7.68) at 418k records / 2,584 tasks; replicated at +12.5% (t=5.09) on a second repo | Fused history arm ships, gated on a configured Gemma-class embedder |
| Semantic fusion on facts | +0.459 useful/1k (p=0.005, Holm-significant), precision +0.025, no token cost, n=121 | Fusion default-on for `recall` and `brief` |
| Locus-scoped retrieval | +59% useful/1k (p=0.027 raw, marginal under Holm), −112 tokens (p<0.001), recall −0.029 | Scoped retrieval shipped; outline kept as a map, not a ranker |

Full rows, task sets and corpus identities are in the [eval ledger](eval_ledger.md).

## Agent outcome: one proof-ready result

Retrieval metrics measure retrieval. Whether a brain changes what an agent
*does* is a different question, and a much harder one to answer honestly.

**One measurement has passed our proof gate.** A correctness task whose decided
value exists only in retained history, run five times per side with
`claude:sonnet:high` in the retained August 2026 panel:

| Condition | Validation pass rate |
| --- | ---: |
| no brain | **0 / 5** |
| semantic_history_brain (history channel) | **5 / 5** |

`proof_ready=true` — the lift survives drop-one — with **0 hard integrity flags**
and 20/20 records provenance-backed across the two tasks in the panel. Without the brain the agent cannot recover
the exact decided value; with it, it reads it from history and restores it.

This flipped the history-channel correctness scope from no-claim to claimable.
It is one task on one repository with n=5 per side, scoped to this runner and
history channel. The other task saturated at 5/5 in both arms and is not proof
of lift. The [retained audit](../benchmarks/agent-brain/evidence/replay-lab-clean/codex-audit-report.md)
and its manifest are checked by `mise run clean-proof:evidence`. This narrow
result does not establish MCP, Radar, codex-runner, or efficiency agent lift.

## What we deliberately do not claim

Brain's benchmark evidence runs under a **claim policy with an auditor that
refuses citations that have not earned them**. Most retained evidence sits in
`no_release_claim` mode on purpose:

```
claim_policy: no_release_claim
proof_ready_comparisons: 0
```

`mise run release:evidence` fails if a claim-bearing suite is not
provenance-complete, audit-clean, backed by a stable proof-ready comparison, and
run at least four times per side against the *current* task definitions.

So the MCP, Radar, codex-runner and efficiency scopes have numbers, and we do
not cite them. They have not passed the gate. The retained artifacts are kept
specifically so an auditor can see why they are not citable yet.

A clean no-claim audit validates the disclosure; it does not establish an
agent-quality improvement. The separate history-channel lane above has its own
proof-required gate.

## Closed negatives

Things we tried, measured, and dropped. A benchmark page with no losses on it
is a marketing page.

- **Query expansion.** An early d≈0.47 was an n≈8 artifact; at n=121 it
  collapsed to d=0.10, p=0.26. Stays opt-in.
- **Model2Vec fusion on history.** Significantly *worse* than BM25 on precision
  at production scale (t=−6.33 on 418k records, t=−2.84 on a second repo) with
  no useful/1k gain. A promising small-repo +31% was noise.
- **Conversation-exchange fusion.** Traded exact-match precision for one extra
  paraphrase hit. Ships dark behind a flag; `query` stays BM25-only.
- **RRF fusion-weight tuning.** Swept; every cell within noise. Equal weight,
  k0=60 stands.
- **Facts FTS5 BM25 as default.** Parity, not better (1.43 vs 1.50). Opt-in.
- **Scoped-floor via backfill facts.** Dead end.

## Head-to-head against other products

We have not run one.

A defensible head-to-head would need the same corpus, the same task set, the
same judge, and the same token accounting on both sides, with enough repetitions
to survive drop-one — the bar our own claim gate applies. Published numbers from
memory products are generally measured on their own corpora with their own
scorers, so quoting them side by side with ours would compare two different
experiments and call it a comparison.

What we can say from measurement rather than assertion:

- **Historical scale costs are substantial**, as [above](#scale-historical-measurements);
  a comparison against another implementation remains unmeasured.
- **Ingest is deterministic and uses no model**, so indexing cost is wall-clock
  and disk rather than tokens. `bench scale` reports both; there is no API bill
  to compare against.
- **Everything here runs locally**, so you can point our benchmarks at your own

## Context recap before the first question

Brain preflight: available (nightly `fac3c90e`), query modes `hybrid|keyword|semantic` exist, facts semantic engine is model2vec RRF. Two caveats recorded: this branch's brain has **no semantic/history/docs index** (brief warned `semantic index missing; run entire brain refresh`), and recall on both this branch and `hosted-sync-client-cor-2030` returned no recorded facts about prior eval designs — the real prior evidence lives in `docs/benchmarks.md` and `docs/eval_ledger.md` instead.

This looks **architectural** (a new experiment/harness, even if it reuses bench infra), so: questions → approaches → spec → plan. Flag me if you want it treated lighter.

**What already exists — your question is partially answered on retrieval metrics:**

| Prior finding (from `docs/benchmarks.md`) | Verdict on record |
|---|---|
| Semantic fusion on **facts** | +0.459 useful/1k, p=0.005, n=121 → shipped default-on |
| Model2Vec fusion on **history** | *worse* than BM25 at 418k records (t=−6.33) → dropped |
| EmbeddingGemma fusion on history | +13% useful/1k → ships gated on a configured embedder |
| Agent outcome | exactly **one** proof-ready result (0/5 → 5/5, history channel, n=5, one task) |

So the open gap isn't "does semantic beat keyword on ranking metrics" — that's been measured both ways per surface. The gap is: **does the semantic stack change what an agent actually does** (task success, tokens, wall clock) enough to pay for the machinery (embedder dependency, index build/refresh, cgo variants, latency, disk). The existing `memory-ladder` and `agent-brain` harnesses give us most of the plumbing for exactly that kind of A/B.

**My one question before proposing approaches — what claim do you want this experiment to settle?**

- **A. Agent-outcome A/B: Brain-with-semantic vs Brain-keyword-only.** Same agent, same tasks, only the retrieval mode differs (`--mode semantic/hybrid` vs `--mode keyword`). Directly answers "does the embedding machinery earn its keep on top of BM25." My recommendation — it isolates exactly the machinery you're doubting.
- **B. Agent-outcome A/B: Brain vs no-Brain-at-all** (grep + git only). Answers "does Brain justify itself," a bigger question than semantic search specifically — and memory-ladder already partially covers it.
- **C. Retrieval-metric replication at current build** — rerun `facts eval` semantic vs keyword on fresh task sets. Cheapest, but it re-answers what the ledger already answered.

Which one (or a different claim)? Also tell me if "machinery" means just the facts-recall embedder path, or the full semantic stack including history/docs/code vectors.

content.text:
Pinned down the machinery split — this matters for the design:

**Two separate pipelines are being conflated, and they have very different costs:**

1. **Facts/memory recall** — embeds each fact at write time with the bundled model2vec (potion-32M, 512-dim). The store here is 24 KB for 5 facts. This is *not* the slow part.
2. **The slow startup embed** — `refresh` (seed/semantic/history/sessions stages): project-file semantic index + history index. That's the 100–200 MB, minutes-long machinery. It feeds `brief`'s semantic context and history search, **not** facts recall. Notably, the ledger already killed model2vec on history (*worse* than BM25 at scale) — history ships BM25-only by default, so part of your suspicion is already confirmed on record.

So "do agents find the right memories with grep" and "is the project-file embed necessary" are two experiments sharing one harness. Here are the approaches:

**Approach A — static retrieval eval (cheap pre-pass).** Reuse `facts eval` with a labeled task set; add a ripgrep baseline runner over facts exported as markdown. Deterministic, no agent tokens. Weakness: it misses your core intuition — an *agent* reformulates queries, so single-shot ranking metrics understate grep.

**Approach B — agentic memory-retrieval A/B (my recommendation).** A `benchmarks/`-style harness (reusing memory-ladder's isolation/shim/grading patterns): same agent, same questions, N reps, arms differing only in the search tool available:
   - `rg`/grep over facts exported as plain markdown (no Brain at all)
   - `entire brain query --keyword` (BM25, no embedder)
   - `entire brain query` hybrid (current default machinery)

   Questions are paraphrase-style (wording deliberately not shared with the fact text — that's semantic's only claimed edge; vocabulary-matching questions make grep win trivially and prove nothing). Gold-labeled facts, deterministic grading: did the right memory reach the answer, at what token/tool-call/wall-clock cost. Corpus at realistic scale (hundreds of facts — 5 is trivially greppable; the agent-brain mined corpora can seed this). Same harness re-runs as **phase 2** against the project-file semantic index: `brief` semantic context vs agentic rg over the worktree, on code-context questions.

**Approach C — end-to-end coding tasks** where needed knowledge lives only in memory (memory-ladder style). Highest validity, but high variance and cost; the ledger shows these need many reps to say anything.

**Recommendation: A as a one-day bounding pre-pass, then B.** If keyword ≈ semantic even in the static eval, agentic grep almost certainly closes the rest. B gives the decision-grade answer: "drop the embedder if the rg arm is within X% success at ≤Y extra tokens."

Does the two-phase scope match your intent (memories first, project-file index second), and is Approach B the shape you want? Also: what's your tolerance threshold — would you drop the machinery at parity, or only if grep is strictly no worse on success *and* tokens?

Eval runs a held-out task set through a selected retriever and reports, per task and
	in aggregate: retrieved items, estimated tokens, precision, recall when labels
	exist for that retriever, and useful-items-per-1k-tokens (the headline agent
	metric).

The tasks file is a JSON array:
  [{"id":"t1","task":"how does X work","branch":"main","k":10,
    "relevant":["fact:abc","fact:def"],"label_source":"human"}]
			With retriever-specific "relevant" ids, metrics are deterministic. Generated
			source-session labels give source-match credit for history/preprocessed-session
			arms but do not define recall. Without labels, pass --judge to have the agent
			decide relevance per surfaced item. With source-session tasks, pass
			--judge --judge-source-matches to replace source-overlap proxy credit with
			judge-labeled relevance for history/preprocessed-session arms.

Usage:
  entire-brain facts eval --tasks <file> [flags]

Flags:
      --agent string                Judge/expand agent: auto, codex, claude-code, ollama, or command (default "auto")
      --agent-command stringArray   Agent command argv for --agent command
      --arm string                  Fact retrieval arm: flat, scoped, scoped-floor, or outline (default "flat")
      --branch string               Default branch for tasks that omit one (default: current branch)
      --expand                      Expand each task query with agent-generated retrieval terms before retrieval
      --expand-cache string         Persist/reuse query expansions at this path
  -h, --help                        help for eval
      --json                        Emit the summary as JSON
      --judge                       Use the agent to judge relevance when a task has no labels
      --judge-cache string          Persist/reuse judge verdicts at this path so re-runs are deterministic and cheap
      --judge-source-matches        With --judge, judge source-match proxy rows instead of counting transcript/session overlap as relevance
      --k int                       Facts to retrieve per task (default 10)
      --model string                Model for codex/claude-code/ollama judge and expand calls
      --retriever string            Retrieval arm: facts, history, query, or raw-sessions (default "facts")
      --semantic                    Rerank with the local embedding backend (RRF fusion of lexical + semantic)
      --tasks string                Path to the held-out task set (JSON array)
DONE
eval-gen turns the brain into a self-labeled benchmark: each captured session
	becomes a task (its opening user request), and the facts whose provenance points
	back to that session are provenance/silver labels. These labels are useful for
	recall-oriented measurement, but hand labels or --refine are still required
	before precision/recall release claims. Each task is tagged with a query-type
	stratum (code/convention/howto/concept). Emits a tasks.json consumable by
	'facts eval --tasks'.

	--source sessions emits tasks directly from exported sessions, including sessions
	with zero distilled facts. Those tasks have source anchors but no relevance labels,
	so use --judge or human labels before making relevance claims.

	--refine judge-filters each task's provenance label set with the agent, keeping
only facts genuinely relevant to the request — trading the recall-oriented "every
session fact" labels for precision-clean ones (verdicts cached for reuse).

Usage:
  entire-brain facts eval-gen [flags]

Flags:
      --agent string                Agent for --refine: auto, codex, claude-code, ollama, or command (default "auto")
      --agent-command stringArray   Agent command argv for --agent command
      --branch string               Limit to one branch (default: all branches with facts)
  -h, --help                        help for eval-gen
      --judge-cache string          Persist/reuse --refine verdicts at this path
      --limit int                   Cap the number of tasks, sampled evenly across strata (0 = all)
      --max-facts int               Skip broad sessions with more relevant facts than this (diffuse targets); 0 = no cap (default 30)
      --min-facts int               Minimum relevant facts for a session to become a task (default 2)
      --model string                Model for codex/claude-code/ollama refine calls
      --out string                  Write tasks JSON to this file (default: stdout)

# Experiment brief — Phase A: static retrieval eval, semantic vs lexical vs grep on durable facts

## Research question

For memory recall over durable facts, does Brain's local semantic machinery (bundled potion-retrieval-32M embeddings + RRF fusion) retrieve the right memories materially better than (1) Brain's lexical-only retrieval, and (2) plain ripgrep over facts exported as Markdown files? If not, the embedder can be dropped from the facts path.

Explicitly out of scope for Phase A: the slow startup project-file embed (`refresh index`/`seed`) — facts recall never touches it; that's Phase 2. History is already BM25-only by default (ledger, 2026-06-10), so no new measurement needed there.

## Arms

All single-shot, k=10, same task set, same corpus:

| Arm | Machinery exercised | What dropping it would mean |
|---|---|---|
| A1 `facts eval` (default, lexical) | Brain fact index, no embedder | baseline |
| A2 `facts eval --semantic` | + model2vec RRF fusion (shipped config) | A2≤A1 → delete embedder from facts path |
| A3 rg baseline | none — script over `entire brain facts files` Markdown export | A3≈A1 → the fact *index* itself is questionable |

A3 runner (new, ~50-line script): tokenize the query, drop stopwords, `rg -i -c` each term over the exported fact files, rank facts by summed term hits, take top 10, emit the same JSON shape as `facts eval` so `eval-compare` works. Deliberately naive — it models the first grep an agent would type, and is a **lower bound** on agentic grep (an agent reformulates; this can't).

## Corpus

This repo's live brain, rebuilt to realistic scale: `entire brain refresh` (sessions export) + facts backfill/distillation, targeting **≥100 distilled facts** (current store has 5 authored facts — unusable; the ledger's prior facts result was n=121 tasks on a live brain). Record exact corpus identity (fact count, branch, store state) per ledger convention. If distillation can't reach ~100 facts here, stop and reassess corpus choice before running — an underpowered run is worse than no run.

## Task set

`facts eval-gen --refine`: each captured session's opening user request becomes a task; facts with provenance to that session are the gold labels; `--refine` judge-filters the label set to precision-clean (verdicts cached → all subsequent eval runs deterministic and model-free). Tasks come pre-stratified (code/convention/howto/concept).

**Key added control — lexical-overlap stratification:** for each task, compute token overlap between the query and its gold facts' text, and report every metric split into high-overlap and low-overlap strata. High-overlap tasks are where grep trivially wins; **low-overlap (paraphrase-like) tasks are semantic's entire claimed edge.** If semantic doesn't win *there*, it wins nowhere.

## Metrics and analysis

- Headline: **useful-items-per-1k-tokens**; also precision@10, recall@10, per stratum.
- Paired per-task deltas, Wilcoxon + Holm correction (ledger convention). Target n ≥100 tasks.
- Reference point: the 2026-06-09 ledger row (+0.459 useful/1k, p=0.005, n=121, default-on decision). If we fail to reproduce a semantic win, investigate before concluding — corpus differences are real but a sign flip needs an explanation.

## Cost ledger (the other half of "justify")

Measured on the same corpus: embedder load time, per-fact embed time at `remember`, vectors store size, and the cgo/no-cgo build surface — vs zero for A3. (Expected to be small for facts; the point is to put the facts-path machinery cost on record separately from the big project-file index cost.)

## Pre-registered decision rule (confirm or adjust the thresholds)

- **Drop embedder from facts path** if A2−A1 < +0.3 useful/1k overall **or** not Holm-significant **or** not positive on the low-overlap stratum.
- **Open a "drop the fact index" question** (not a decision — A3 is single-shot only) if A3 is within 10% of A1 on useful/1k.
- **Keep machinery, proceed to Phase B (agentic A/B)** only if A2 clears all three bars — a static win still must survive an agent that can reformulate queries before the machinery is truly justified.

## Threats to validity

- `--refine` labels are agent-judged (cached). Silver, not human — fine for a drop decision, stated plainly in the ledger row.
- Single corpus, one repo. If the result gates an actual code removal, replicate on a second repo first (ledger convention).
- A3's naivety cuts one way only: if naive grep already matches Brain, agentic grep is a fortiori ≥. The reverse (grep loses) proves little — hence Phase B.

## Deliverables

`tasks.json`, per-arm eval JSONs + `eval-compare` outputs, the rg-runner script, cost measurements, and a draft eval-ledger row. Spec/artifacts live in `.context/` (not committed — per your no-committed-docs rule); harness script placement TBD on approval.

---

Two things to confirm: the decision thresholds (+0.3 useful/1k for the embedder, 10% for the index), and whether rebuilding this repo's brain (refresh + distillation — costs agent tokens) is acceptable as the corpus-build step, or you'd rather point at a different repo with an existing rich brain.

yes thats fine rebuild if needed. have a good representative sample. 

then i think we need some number of real queries that agents would issue and then run them in parallel using brain semantic search tools and standard tools.

Approved — and your addition is exactly what the task set gives us: `eval-gen` tasks are *real* agent queries (each is the opening user request of a captured session), and each query runs through all three arms in parallel: Brain semantic, Brain lexical, plain rg. The live-agent version (agents iterating with their own tool choices) stays Phase B if semantic survives Phase A.

Saving the approved brief to `.context/`, then starting the corpus rebuild. First, discovering the distillation command surface.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""A3 arm: naive ripgrep retrieval over `entire brain facts files` Markdown export.

Emits a `facts eval --json`-shaped summary so eval-compare can consume it.
Deliberately naive: models the first grep an agent would type (lower bound on
agentic grep). Scoring: rank facts by distinct query terms matched (rg -i -w),
tiebreak by total match count.
"""

import argparse
import hashlib
import json
import re
import subprocess
import sys
import tempfile
import time
from pathlib import Path

STOPWORDS = set(
    """a an and are as at be by can do does for from has have how i in is it of
    on or that the this to was we what when where which why will with you your
    our it's dont don't should would could did done about into over under""".split()
)


def tokenize(text):
    terms = re.findall(r"[A-Za-z0-9_]{2,}", text.lower())
    seen, out = set(), []
    for t in terms:
        if t in STOPWORDS or t in seen:
            continue
        seen.add(t)
        out.append(t)
    return out


def parse_fact_file(path: Path):
    raw = path.read_text()
    m = re.match(r"^---\n(.*?)\n---\n(.*)$", raw, re.DOTALL)
    if not m:
        return None
    front, body = m.groups()
    meta = {}
    for line in front.splitlines():
        if ":" in line:
            k, v = line.split(":", 1)
            meta[k.strip()] = v.strip()
    return {
        "id": meta.get("id", ""),
        "paths": meta.get("paths", ""),
        "text": body.strip(),
        "file": str(path),
    }


def load_facts(facts_dir: Path):
    facts = []
    for p in sorted(facts_dir.rglob("fact-*.md")):
        f = parse_fact_file(p)
        if f and f["id"]:
            facts.append(f)
    return facts


def rg_term_counts(term, facts_dir: Path):
    """path -> match count for one term, whole-word, case-insensitive."""
    try:
        out = subprocess.run(
            ["rg", "--count-matches", "-i", "-w", "-F", term, "-g", "fact-*.md", str(facts_dir)],
            capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=30,
        ).stdout
    except FileNotFoundError:
        sys.exit("ripgrep (rg) not found on PATH")
    counts = {}
    for line in out.splitlines():
        path, _, n = line.rpartition(":")
        if path:
            counts[path] = int(n)
    return counts


def retrieve(task_text, facts, facts_dir, k):
    terms = tokenize(task_text)
    scores = {}  # file -> [distinct terms, total matches]
    for t in terms:
        for path, n in rg_term_counts(t, facts_dir).items():
            s = scores.setdefault(path, [0, 0])
            s[0] += 1
            s[1] += n
    by_file = {f["file"]: f for f in facts}
    ranked = sorted(
        (f for f in scores if f in by_file),
        key=lambda f: (-scores[f][0], -scores[f][1], f),
    )
    return [by_file[f] for f in ranked[:k]]


def estimate_tokens(items):
    # mirrors internal/cli/facts_eval.go estimateTokens exactly
    chars = sum(len(f["text"]) + len(f["paths"]) + 4 for f in items)
    return (chars + 3) // 4


def run_eval(tasks_path: Path, facts_root: Path, k, retriever_name="rg-baseline"):
    tasks = json.loads(tasks_path.read_text())
    branch_dirs = {}

    def facts_for_branch(branch):
        if branch not in branch_dirs:
            d = facts_root / branch if (facts_root / branch).is_dir() else facts_root
            branch_dirs[branch] = (d, load_facts(d))
        return branch_dirs[branch]

    results = []
    for t in tasks:
        d, facts = facts_for_branch(t.get("branch", ""))
        kk = t.get("k") or k
        t0 = time.monotonic()
        surfaced = retrieve(t["task"], facts, d, kk)
        latency_ms = int((time.monotonic() - t0) * 1000)
        relevant = set(t.get("relevant") or [])
        hit = sum(1 for f in surfaced if f["id"] in relevant)
        tokens = estimate_tokens(surfaced)
        precision = hit / len(surfaced) if surfaced else 0.0
        recall = hit / len(relevant) if relevant else 0.0
        results.append({
            "id": t["id"],
            "task": t["task"],
            "query_type": t.get("query_type", ""),
            "retriever": retriever_name,
            "relevance_source": "explicit_label",
            "surfaced": len(surfaced),
            "tokens": tokens,
            "latency_ms": latency_ms,
            "expansion_latency_ms": 0,
            "end_to_end_latency_ms": latency_ms,
            "relevant_surfaced": hit,
            "precision": precision,
            "recall": recall,
            "useful_per_1k": (hit / tokens * 1000) if tokens else 0.0,
            "labeled": bool(relevant),
            "label_source": t.get("label_source", ""),
        })

    n = len(results)
    mean = lambda key: sum(r[key] for r in results) / n if n else 0.0
    strata = {}
    for r in results:
        strata.setdefault(r["query_type"] or "unknown", []).append(r)
    by_stratum = {
        s: {
            "tasks": len(rs),
            "mean_tokens": sum(r["tokens"] for r in rs) / len(rs),
            "mean_precision": sum(r["precision"] for r in rs) / len(rs),
            "mean_useful_per_1k": sum(r["useful_per_1k"] for r in rs) / len(rs),
        }
        for s, rs in strata.items()
    }
    return {
        "retriever": retriever_name,
        "run_config": {
            "tasks_path": str(tasks_path),
            "tasks_sha256": hashlib.sha256(tasks_path.read_bytes()).hexdigest(),
            "k": k,
            "retriever": retriever_name,
            "judge": False,
            "expand": False,
            "semantic": False,
            "label_policy": "explicit_labels_only",
            "raw_session_id_scheme": "",
        },
        "tasks": n,
        "mean_tokens": mean("tokens"),
        "mean_latency_ms": mean("latency_ms"),
        "mean_expansion_latency_ms": 0.0,
        "mean_end_to_end_latency_ms": mean("end_to_end_latency_ms"),
        "mean_precision": mean("precision"),
        "mean_useful_per_1k": mean("useful_per_1k"),
        "by_stratum": by_stratum,
        "results": results,
    }


def self_test():
    with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as td:
        root = Path(td)
        fdir = root / "cat"
        fdir.mkdir()
        mk = lambda name, body: (fdir / name).write_text(
            f"---\nid: fact:{name[5:-3]}\npaths: architecture.test\n---\n\n{body}\n"
        )
        mk("fact-aaa.md", "The sync retry loop uses exponential backoff with jitter.")
        mk("fact-bbb.md", "Database migrations run before the server boots.")
        mk("fact-ccc.md", "Backoff is capped at 30 seconds for sync retries in the loop.")
        tasks = [{
            "id": "t1",
            "task": "how does the sync retry backoff loop work",
            "branch": "",
            "k": 2,
            "relevant": ["fact:aaa", "fact:ccc"],
            "label_source": "human",
        }]
        tp = root / "tasks.json"
        tp.write_text(json.dumps(tasks))
        s = run_eval(tp, root, 2)
        r = s["results"][0]
        got = {r_id for r_id in (f["id"] for f in [])}  # placeholder
        assert r["surfaced"] == 2, r
        assert r["relevant_surfaced"] == 2, r
        assert r["precision"] == 1.0 and r["recall"] == 1.0, r
        assert r["tokens"] > 0 and r["useful_per_1k"] > 0, r
        # fact-bbb shares no query terms and must not outrank the two gold facts
        print("self-test passed")


def main():
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    ap.add_argument("--tasks")
    ap.add_argument("--facts-root", help="facts export dir, or parent of per-branch subdirs")
    ap.add_argument("--k", type=int, default=10)
    ap.add_argument("--out", default="-")
    ap.add_argument("--self-test", action="store_true")
    args = ap.parse_args()
    if args.self_test:
        self_test()
        return
    if not args.tasks or not args.facts_root:
        ap.error("--tasks and --facts-root required")
    summary = run_eval(Path(args.tasks), Path(args.facts_root), args.k)
    out = json.dumps(summary, indent=2)
    if args.out == "-":
        print(out)
    else:
        Path(args.out).write_text(out)
        print(f"wrote {args.out}: {summary['tasks']} tasks, "
              f"mean useful/1k {summary['mean_useful_per_1k']:.3f}", file=sys.stderr)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Paired comparison of two `facts eval --json` summaries (A1 vs A2 vs A3),
overall and stratified by query<->gold-fact lexical overlap.

Overlap per task = max over its gold facts of (fraction of query terms present
in the fact text, whole-word, case-insensitive). Low-overlap tasks are where
semantic retrieval claims its edge.

Stats: paired mean delta, Wilcoxon signed-rank (normal approximation, fine at
n>25) and exact sign test as a robustness check. stdlib only.
"""

import argparse
import json
import math
import sys
from pathlib import Path

sys.path.insert(0, str(Path(__file__).parent))
from rg_eval import load_facts, term_count, tokenize  # noqa: E402

METRICS = ["useful_per_1k", "precision", "recall", "tokens"]


def task_overlap(task, facts_by_id):
    terms = tokenize(task["task"])
    if not terms:
        return 0.0
    best = 0.0
    for fid in task.get("relevant") or []:
        f = facts_by_id.get(fid)
        if not f:
            continue
        hit = sum(1 for t in terms if term_count(t, f["text"]))
        best = max(best, hit / len(terms))
    return best


def wilcoxon(deltas):
    """Signed-rank test, normal approximation, zero-deltas dropped."""
    d = [x for x in deltas if x != 0]
    n = len(d)
    if n < 6:
        return float("nan")
    ranked = sorted(range(n), key=lambda i: abs(d[i]))
    ranks = [0.0] * n
    i = 0
    while i < n:
        j = i
        while j + 1 < n and abs(d[ranked[j + 1]]) == abs(d[ranked[i]]):
            j += 1
        avg = (i + j) / 2 + 1
        for k in range(i, j + 1):
            ranks[ranked[k]] = avg
        i = j + 1
    w_plus = sum(r for x, r in zip(d, ranks) if x > 0)
    mu = n * (n + 1) / 4
    sigma = math.sqrt(n * (n + 1) * (2 * n + 1) / 24)
    if sigma == 0:
        return float("nan")
    z = (w_plus - mu) / sigma
    return 2 * (1 - 0.5 * (1 + math.erf(abs(z) / math.sqrt(2))))


def sign_test(deltas):
    pos = sum(1 for x in deltas if x > 0)
    neg = sum(1 for x in deltas if x < 0)
    n = pos + neg
    if n == 0:
        return float("nan")
    k = min(pos, neg)
    p = sum(math.comb(n, i) for i in range(k + 1)) / 2 ** n
    return min(1.0, 2 * p)


def compare(a_results, b_results, ids):
    a = {r["id"]: r for r in a_results}
    b = {r["id"]: r for r in b_results}
    shared = [i for i in ids if i in a and i in b]
    out = {"n": len(shared)}
    for m in METRICS:
        deltas = [b[i][m] - a[i][m] for i in shared]
        out[m] = {
            "mean_a": sum(a[i][m] for i in shared) / len(shared) if shared else 0,
            "mean_b": sum(b[i][m] for i in shared) / len(shared) if shared else 0,
            "mean_delta": sum(deltas) / len(deltas) if deltas else 0,
            "wilcoxon_p": wilcoxon(deltas),
            "sign_p": sign_test(deltas),
            "wins": sum(1 for x in deltas if x > 0),
            "losses": sum(1 for x in deltas if x < 0),
            "ties": sum(1 for x in deltas if x == 0),
        }
    return out


def main():
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    ap.add_argument("--tasks", required=True)
    ap.add_argument("--facts-root", required=True)
    ap.add_argument("--a", required=True, help="baseline summary (e.g. lexical)")
    ap.add_argument("--b", required=True, help="comparison summary (e.g. semantic)")
    ap.add_argument("--label-a", default="A")
    ap.add_argument("--label-b", default="B")
    ap.add_argument("--overlap-split", type=float, default=None,
                    help="overlap threshold for low/high strata (default: median)")
    args = ap.parse_args()

    tasks = json.loads(Path(args.tasks).read_text())
    root = Path(args.facts_root)
    facts_by_branch = {}
    facts_by_id = {}
    for t in tasks:
        br = t.get("branch", "")
        if br not in facts_by_branch:
            d = root / br if (root / br).is_dir() else root
            facts_by_branch[br] = load_facts(d)
        for f in facts_by_branch[br]:
            facts_by_id[f["id"]] = f

    overlaps = {t["id"]: task_overlap(t, facts_by_id) for t in tasks}
    vals = sorted(overlaps.values())
    split = args.overlap_split if args.overlap_split is not None else vals[len(vals) // 2]
    low = [i for i, v in overlaps.items() if v < split]
    high = [i for i, v in overlaps.items() if v >= split]

    a = json.loads(Path(args.a).read_text())["results"]
    b = json.loads(Path(args.b).read_text())["results"]
    all_ids = list(overlaps)

    report = {
        "comparison": f"{args.label_b} - {args.label_a}",
        "overlap_split": split,
        "overall": compare(a, b, all_ids),
        "low_overlap": compare(a, b, low),
        "high_overlap": compare(a, b, high),
    }
    print(json.dumps(report, indent=2))

    o = report["overall"]["useful_per_1k"]
    lo = report["low_overlap"]["useful_per_1k"]
    print(f"\n{args.label_b} vs {args.label_a}: useful/1k delta "
          f"{o['mean_delta']:+.3f} (p={o['wilcoxon_p']:.4f}, "
          f"{o['wins']}W/{o['losses']}L/{o['ties']}T, n={report['overall']['n']}); "
          f"low-overlap delta {lo['mean_delta']:+.3f} "
          f"(p={lo['wilcoxon_p']:.4f}, n={report['low_overlap']['n']})",
          file=sys.stderr)


def self_test():
    assert sign_test([1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1]) < 0.01
    assert sign_test([1, -1, 1, -1]) == 1.0
    p = wilcoxon([1.0, 2.0, 1.5, 2.5, 1.2, 1.8, 2.2, 1.1, 0.9, 1.4])
    assert p < 0.01, p
    p2 = wilcoxon([1, -1, 2, -2, 3, -3, 1.5, -1.5])
    assert p2 > 0.5, p2
    print("self-test passed")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    if "--self-test" in sys.argv:
        self_test()
    else:
        main()

# Phase A results — grep is embarrassingly competitive

**Headline: naive grep over exported fact files statistically tied Brain's semantic retrieval on the headline metric, and significantly beat Brain's lexical mode. Semantic's machinery survived on exactly one metric: recall.**

Corpus: 255 sessions distilled → 1,342 facts; 65 judge-refined tasks built from real session opening requests; k=10; all three arms ran the same queries.

| Arm | useful/1k | precision | recall | query latency |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Brain lexical | 1.550 | 0.111 | 0.247 | 14 ms |
| Brain semantic (shipped default) | 1.995 | 0.137 | 0.361 | 16 ms |
| grep over `facts files` export | **2.213** | **0.141** | 0.301 | 44 ms |

What the paired stats say:

- **Semantic vs lexical**: +0.445 useful/1k, p=0.0002 — real, and it replicates the June ledger row (+0.459) almost exactly. The shipped default isn't fake.
- **Grep vs lexical**: +0.663, p=0.0003 — grep significantly beats Brain's own lexical mode. The pre-registered "question the fact index" trigger (grep within 10%) fired with huge headroom.
- **Grep vs semantic**: useful/1k and precision are statistical ties (p=0.71, 19W/21L/25T). But **semantic wins recall** (+0.060, p=0.025): on low-overlap (paraphrase-style) tasks grep *never* beat it on recall (0W/5L/25T). Semantic reaches facts whose wording doesn't share terms with the query; that reachability is the one thing the embedder demonstrably buys.

What this means for "too much machinery":

- **Facts embeddings are not the expensive part anyway**: 1.7 MB of vectors for 878 facts, +2 ms per query, embedded incrementally at write time. Dropping them saves almost nothing and costs measurable recall.
- **The slow startup embed you complained about (project-file semantic index) was never exercised by memory recall at all** — this phase confirms facts recall doesn't need it. Its justification remains unestablished; that's Phase 2's question and it's where the real machinery savings live.
- **The uncomfortable finding is the fact *index***: a 65-line grep script over the Markdown export outperformed Brain's lexical retrieval outright. Whether an *agent* with iterative grep closes semantic's recall gap is exactly Phase B — and after this result I'd say Phase B is warranted before any keep/drop decision.

Caveats: n=65 (eval-gen found only 65 sessions with ≥2 refined facts; I targeted 100), single corpus, silver labels, recall win is raw p not Holm-corrected. One repo says "open question," not "ship a deletion."

Everything is reproducible in `.context/semantic-eval/` (tasks, per-arm JSONs, comparisons, scripts); spec updated with results; finding recorded as durable fact `fact:b14415c79fcc48f7298fbb76`. Want me to design Phase B (agents iterating queries, grep vs brain tools), or replicate Phase A on a second repo first?

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Phase B: agentic memory-retrieval A/B.

Same tasks as Phase A, live Claude Code agent per (task, arm), budget-matched:
  arm grep  — standard tools (Read/Grep/Glob) over the facts Markdown export
  arm brain — Bash restricted to `entire brain query` (shipped hybrid retrieval)

The agent must output fact IDs; grading is deterministic against the task's
judge-refined gold labels. Sandboxes live outside the repo so no project
hooks/CLAUDE.md load into the runs.

Usage:
  python3 phase_b.py --tasks tasks.json --facts-root facts-export \
      --out runs-b/ [--arms grep,brain] [--jobs 4] [--limit 0] [--model sonnet]
Re-runs skip (task, arm) pairs that already have a result file.
"""

import argparse
import concurrent.futures
import json
import re
import shutil
import subprocess
import sys
import tempfile
import time
from pathlib import Path

BUDGET_USD = "0.25"
TOOLCALL_HINT = 12

PROMPT = """A developer is about to start this task in the entire-brain repository (branch: {branch}):

"{task}"

Durable memories (facts) distilled from past agent sessions exist for this repository. Your job: find the facts most relevant to this task.

{arm_instructions}

Work within about {hint} tool calls. When done, output your answer as a line `FACTS:` followed by up to 10 fact IDs (format `fact:<hex>`), one per line, most relevant first. Output nothing after the list."""

ARM_GREP = """The facts are Markdown files in your current directory (one file per fact, organized by topic). Each file has frontmatter with its `id:` and the fact text as body. Search them with your file tools (Grep, Glob, Read)."""

ARM_BRAIN = """Search the facts with the brain query CLI (the only tool you may use):

    entire brain query --json --source fact --branch {branch} --limit 10 "<your query>"

It returns ranked facts with ids. You may run it multiple times with different queries."""


def run_one(task, arm, facts_root: Path, out_dir: Path, model):
    rid = f"{task['id']}--{arm}"
    out_file = out_dir / f"{rid}.json"
    if out_file.exists():
        return rid, "cached"
    branch = task.get("branch", "main")
    with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory(prefix="semeval-b-") as td:
        cwd = Path(td) / "work"
        cwd.mkdir()
        if arm == "grep":
            src = facts_root / branch if (facts_root / branch).is_dir() else facts_root
            shutil.copytree(src, cwd, dirs_exist_ok=True)
            arm_instructions = ARM_GREP
            allowed = "Read Grep Glob"
        else:
            arm_instructions = ARM_BRAIN.format(branch=branch)
            allowed = '"Bash(entire brain query:*)"'
        prompt = PROMPT.format(task=task["task"], branch=branch,
                               arm_instructions=arm_instructions, hint=TOOLCALL_HINT)
        t0 = time.monotonic()
        try:
            proc = subprocess.run(
                ["claude", "-p", prompt, "--model", model,
                 "--output-format", "json",
                 "--max-budget-usd", BUDGET_USD,
                 "--permission-mode", "dontAsk",
                 "--allowedTools", *allowed.replace('"', "").split(),
                 "--disallowedTools", "Agent", "Task", "WebSearch", "WebFetch"],
                capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=600, cwd=cwd,
            )
            wall = time.monotonic() - t0
            try:
                payload = json.loads(proc.stdout)
            except json.JSONDecodeError:
                payload = {"result": proc.stdout, "parse_error": True}
        except subprocess.TimeoutExpired:
            payload = {"result": "", "timeout": True}
            wall = time.monotonic() - t0
            proc = None
        record = {
            "id": task["id"], "arm": arm, "branch": branch, "task": task["task"],
            "relevant": task.get("relevant") or [],
            "wall_s": round(wall, 1),
            "exit_code": proc.returncode if proc else -1,
            "stderr_tail": (proc.stderr[-500:] if proc else ""),
            "payload": payload,
        }
        out_file.write_text(json.dumps(record, indent=1))
    return rid, "done"


def main():
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    ap.add_argument("--tasks", required=True)
    ap.add_argument("--facts-root", required=True)
    ap.add_argument("--out", required=True)
    ap.add_argument("--arms", default="grep,brain")
    ap.add_argument("--jobs", type=int, default=4)
    ap.add_argument("--limit", type=int, default=0)
    ap.add_argument("--model", default="sonnet")
    args = ap.parse_args()

    tasks = json.loads(Path(args.tasks).read_text())
    if args.limit:
        tasks = tasks[: args.limit]
    out_dir = Path(args.out)
    out_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    facts_root = Path(args.facts_root).resolve()
    arms = args.arms.split(",")

    jobs = [(t, a) for t in tasks for a in arms]
    print(f"{len(jobs)} runs ({len(tasks)} tasks x {arms}), budget ${BUDGET_USD}/run",
          file=sys.stderr)
    done = 0
    with concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=args.jobs) as ex:
        futs = [ex.submit(run_one, t, a, facts_root, out_dir, args.model) for t, a in jobs]
        for f in concurrent.futures.as_completed(futs):
            rid, state = f.result()
            done += 1
            print(f"[{done}/{len(jobs)}] {rid}: {state}", file=sys.stderr, flush=True)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Grade Phase B runs: per-task recall/precision of reported fact IDs vs gold
labels, plus token cost; paired Wilcoxon across arms."""

import json
import re
import sys
from pathlib import Path

sys.path.insert(0, str(Path(__file__).parent))
from analyze import wilcoxon, sign_test  # noqa: E402

FACT_RE = re.compile(r"fact:[0-9a-f]{6,}")


def grade_record(rec):
    text = rec["payload"].get("result") or ""
    tail = text.split("FACTS:")[-1] if "FACTS:" in text else text
    reported = []
    for m in FACT_RE.findall(tail):
        if m not in reported:
            reported.append(m)
    reported = reported[:10]
    gold = set(rec["relevant"])
    hit = sum(1 for r in reported if r in gold)
    usage = rec["payload"].get("usage") or {}
    tokens = sum(usage.get(k, 0) for k in
                 ("input_tokens", "output_tokens",
                  "cache_creation_input_tokens", "cache_read_input_tokens"))
    return {
        "id": rec["id"], "arm": rec["arm"],
        "reported": len(reported), "hit": hit,
        "precision": hit / len(reported) if reported else 0.0,
        "recall": hit / len(gold) if gold else 0.0,
        "tokens": tokens,
        "cost_usd": rec["payload"].get("total_cost_usd", 0.0),
        "turns": rec["payload"].get("num_turns", 0),
        "wall_s": rec["wall_s"],
        "failed": bool(rec["payload"].get("timeout") or rec["payload"].get("parse_error")
                       or rec["exit_code"] != 0),
    }


def main():
    runs_dir = Path(sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else "runs-b")
    rows = [grade_record(json.loads(p.read_text())) for p in sorted(runs_dir.glob("*.json"))]
    ok = [r for r in rows if not r["failed"]]
    failed = [r for r in rows if r["failed"]]
    arms = sorted({r["arm"] for r in ok})
    by_arm = {a: {r["id"]: r for r in ok if r["arm"] == a} for a in arms}

    print(f"{len(rows)} runs, {len(failed)} failed/excluded")
    for a in arms:
        rs = list(by_arm[a].values())
        n = len(rs)
        m = lambda k: sum(r[k] for r in rs) / n
        print(f"  {a:6s} n={n} recall={m('recall'):.3f} precision={m('precision'):.3f} "
              f"tokens={m('tokens'):.0f} cost=${m('cost_usd'):.4f} "
              f"turns={m('turns'):.1f} wall={m('wall_s'):.0f}s")

    if len(arms) == 2:
        a, b = arms

Verdict: embedder on facts survives Phase A on recall only; fact index vs

## Expanded Phase A (pooled, 2026-10-12)

User asked for n>=100. entire-brain tops out at 79 refine-surviving tasks, so
a second corpus was added: marvin (103 sessions -> 376 facts -> 70 tasks).
Pooled n=149. Facts fact:b14415c79fcc48f7298fbb76 (Phase A),
fact:fff3f03d8fd0b36a40c03ffa (Phase B). Pooled results
(pooled-analysis.json):

- semantic vs lexical: +0.358 useful/1k p<0.0001; holds in low-overlap
  (+0.121, p=0.028). Replicated per-repo (entire-brain +0.445 p=0.0002;
  marvin +0.277 p=0.0006 — note marvin is under the +0.3 bar alone).
- grep vs semantic: useful/1k and precision dead ties (p=0.84/0.89);
  semantic wins recall (+0.051 p=0.0045; low-overlap +0.083 p=0.0058).
- grep vs lexical: +0.376 p<0.0001 — naive grep beats brain lexical on
  both repos.

## Phase B results (agentic A/B, 2026-10-12)

149 tasks x 2 arms, sonnet, $0.60 budget cap (0 exhausted), 0 failures.
Arms: Bash restricted to `entire brain query` vs Read/Grep/Glob over the
markdown export. Grading: fact IDs in final answer vs judge-refined gold.
NOTE: first brain-arm batch was invalid (allowedTools quoting bug denied the
tool; caught because recall was exactly 0 at turns=3) and was re-run after a
verified fix.

| Arm | recall | precision | tokens | cost | wall |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| brain query | 0.629 | 0.278 | 218k | $0.193 | 33s |
| grep export | 0.565 | 0.266 | 324k | $0.245 | 49s |

- Accuracy: marginal, not significant (recall p=0.071, precision p=0.051).
- Efficiency: brain decisive (+105k tokens p<0.0001, +$0.052, +16s for grep).
- Agentic grep CLOSED the paraphrase gap (low-overlap recall tie p=0.88);
  brain's edge concentrates in high-overlap tasks (p=0.0075) and the smaller
  corpus (marvin p=0.042).

## Conclusions

1. Facts semantic embedder: cheap (1.7 MB / 878 facts, +2 ms) and it is what
   makes the fact index better than grep. Keep if the index stays.
2. Brain lexical-only is strictly worse than naive grep — index-without-

# Final results — Phases A and B, pooled n=149 across two repos

**Bottom line: the semantic machinery's measurable value to an agent is efficiency, not accuracy. And the config you'd reach by "dropping the embedder but keeping the index" is the single worst option measured.**

## Phase A (static retrieval, n=149: entire-brain 79 + marvin 70)

| Comparison | useful/1k | verdict |
|---|---|---|
| semantic vs lexical | +0.358, p<0.0001 | semantic wins, replicated on both repos |
| grep vs semantic | +0.018, p=0.84 | dead tie (semantic keeps a small recall edge, p=0.0045) |
| grep vs lexical | +0.376, p<0.0001 | **naive grep beats Brain's lexical mode** |

## Phase B (live agents, 149 tasks × 2 arms, sonnet, budget-matched)

| Arm | recall | precision | tokens/run | cost/run | wall |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `entire brain query` | 0.629 | 0.278 | 218k | $0.193 | 33s |
| grep over markdown export | 0.565 | 0.266 | 324k | $0.245 | 49s |

Accuracy differences are marginal (recall p=0.071, precision p=0.051). The decisive difference is cost: **grep burns +48% tokens and +50% wall time per memory lookup** (p<0.0001) because it iterates ~16 turns against the brain arm's 8. And notably, the iterating agent *fully closed* the paraphrase-recall gap that was semantic's one static edge (low-overlap recall: tie, p=0.88) — brain's remaining win concentrates where grep drowns in matches (high-overlap, p=0.0075) and on the smaller corpus.

## What this says about the machinery

1. **Facts embedder: keep it if you keep the index.** It costs almost nothing (1.7 MB vectors, +2 ms/query, bundled model) and it's the only reason the index beats grep at all.
2. **Never ship index-without-embedder** — Brain's keyword mode loses to a 65-line grep script on both repos.
3. **The fact index earns ~105k tokens + 16 s per lookup, not better answers.** Whether ~$0.05/lookup justifies the pipeline is a product-volume call, now with numbers attached.
4. **Your original complaint — the slow startup project-file embed — was never touched by memory recall in any of this.** Neither phase justifies it. If you want a Phase 2 on that pipeline (brief semantic context vs agentic rg over the worktree), the harness is ready to be pointed at it.

# Does Brain's semantic search justify its machinery? — Experiment summary

## Question

Can an agent find the right durable memories with plain grep over exported fact files as well as it can with Brain's retrieval stack (fact index + bundled model2vec embedder + RRF fusion)? If yes, the indexing/embedding machinery on the facts path can be dropped.

## Method

- **Corpora:** rebuilt live brains for two repos — entire-brain (255 sessions → 1,342 facts) and marvin (103 sessions → 376 facts).
- **Tasks:** 149 real agent queries (each the opening user request of a captured session), gold-labeled by provenance and judge-refined. 149 is the honest ceiling: sessions whose labels failed refinement are unanswerable and were excluded rather than padded.
- **Phase A (static):** every query run single-shot at k=10 through three arms — Brain lexical, Brain semantic (shipped config), and a deliberately naive grep scorer over `entire brain facts files` Markdown export. Paired Wilcoxon, stratified by query↔fact lexical overlap.
- **Phase B (agentic):** one live sonnet agent per (task, arm), budget-matched, 298 runs. Arm 1: only tool is `entire brain query`. Arm 2: only tools are Read/Grep/Glob over the export. Graded on fact IDs in the final answer.

## Phase A results (n=149)

| Comparison | useful/1k delta | p | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| semantic vs lexical | +0.358 | <0.0001 | semantic wins, replicated on both repos |
| grep vs semantic | +0.018 | 0.84 | tie; semantic keeps a recall edge (+0.051, p=0.0045) on paraphrase tasks |
| grep vs lexical | +0.376 | <0.0001 | naive grep beats Brain's lexical mode |

## Phase B results (149 tasks × 2 arms)

| Arm | recall | precision | tokens/run | cost/run | wall |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| brain query | 0.629 | 0.278 | 218k | $0.193 | 33s |
| grep export | 0.565 | 0.266 | 324k | $0.245 | 49s |

Accuracy: not significant (recall p=0.071, precision p=0.051). Efficiency: decisive — grep needs +48% tokens and +50% wall time (p<0.0001) because it iterates ~16 turns vs 8. The iterating agent fully closed semantic's paraphrase-recall edge from Phase A (low-overlap recall tie, p=0.88); brain's remaining advantage sits in high-overlap tasks (p=0.0075) and the smaller corpus (p=0.042).

## Conclusions

1. **The embedder on facts is cheap and load-bearing**: 1.7 MB vectors, +2 ms/query — and it's the only reason the index beats grep at all. Keep it if the index stays.
2. **Index-without-embedder is the worst configuration**: Brain's keyword-only mode loses to a 65-line grep script on both repos. Don't "simplify" to it.
3. **The fact index buys efficiency, not accuracy**: ~105k tokens and ~16 s saved per memory lookup, equal answers. At ~$0.05/lookup it justifies itself on query volume — a product call, now with numbers.
4. **The slow startup project-file embed — your original complaint — was never exercised by memory recall in either phase.** Nothing measured here justifies it. It needs its own experiment (Phase 2) or removal from the default path.

## Caveats

One model (sonnet), one rep per task/arm, judge-refined silver labels, two repos, one machine. The first Phase B brain-arm batch was invalid (runner bug denied the agent its tool); it was fixed, verified, and fully re-run — reported numbers are from the valid batch.
